en: Straight that does what is hidden.
If you look at that infidel,
His face is like iron,
It is as big as a mountain.
Relax the front man,
Like a scum bag,
His eyes are like a burning flame.
Like a lot of iron,
There is a naked type.
He who ruled the universe,
You see, there is such a madman.
Go personal,
Fire came out of both eyes,
The embers came out of the furnace,
If he shouts in anger,
He left humanity
If you fight now,
The moon has passed through the universe.
Descendant of Er Manas
Because of courage.
When it comes to personal
The people ran and shouted,
Disappointed by the population,
There was a big conflict.
How many Sarybay,
He sucked like a dragon.
Seitek, son of Semetei
To die if it really comes to death,
Son of a monster, you infidel,
Face to face to shed blood,
He started to get angry.
It just came alive again,
In the gated courtyard,
In the protection of Kanykey,
A big conflict, a big trouble
Raised the white flag
There was a noise in the sky,
He roared with force.
Expanded Talas
He stepped on the roof.
Disbelieve in shame,
Roaring in anger,
Saying different things
Of the person who saw it
Azat roared throughout.
Flashing like lightning,
Where is your place to hang out?
Sarybay remains in disgust
It was private.
Looking guilty
Humanity is a slave
The price of kefir is divided,
Get used to what you say,
Give me my fee -
He was angry,
Bubbling and raging,
He beat the drum.
The drum beat,
The month of the month
Hungry cry, sly suran
There was a loud noise,
The son of a monster is an infidel
He shouted in private.
The warrior turned his mouth,
All of the universe
Now it's like slaughtering,
It was private.
The violence is like a mountain,
Eighteen thousand universes
Like eating while driving.
His face is like iron,
Go personal,
He who set fire to grassy lands,
Who stirred the stars in the heavens.
With the fortune of holy Kyzyr
He had been friends from the very beginning—
He was that lion himself.
None facing him had won,
No foe had dared confront him,
No man opposing him had prevailed.
“Forefather Tügöl Khan,
Keep your all-seeing eye upon me,” he said;
“First forefather Baary Khan,
Come and be my companion,” he said.
Praying to his ancestors,
Your mighty wretch, brimming with strength,
Prepared himself with Kerkula.
His opponent was Sarybay,
An infidel of perfect strength,
A hero of boundless courage.
If fate had decreed his death,
He would ride straight forth and thrust his spear;
Against the raging infidel
He would stake his life and wage war,
And save all the people
From death.
Thus he rode out for single combat.
Hero Seytek stood upon the rise;
Sarybay charged and struck.
When Sarybay thrust his spear,
It could not withstand the contest:
Sarybay’s spear
Burst apart into ten pieces,
Shattering utterly.
Hero Seytek did not even lean;
Sarybay swerved aside.
He struck Kerkula on the thigh,
Then took the ornate spear in hand.
Your hero Seytek stretched tall:
“This side of the belt,” he said,
“The lower edge of the lung,” he said,
“This is the measured spot,” he said,
And staked his life upon a hair.
His opponent was Sarybay;
His only prayer was to God—
Such was the nature of the clash.
His adversary was Sarybay;
To face him and test himself,
On the good path granted by the Creator,
To surrender his precious life,
To stand face-to-face,
In battle where blood would flow,
To behold a hero’s courage,
And, if God so willed,
To give up his dear life,
He made ready all his weapons,
And bound on Ajybay’s sharp steel blade
Without its scabbard.
Arming and preparing himself,
He prayed to the spirit of the noble lord
Who had passed into the other world.
Behold the valor inherited
From his fathers and forefathers.
His forefather was Tügöl Khan,
Blessed by Kydyr from the beginning;
His first ancestor was Baary Khan,
Blessed by Kydyr from birth.
The more they were spent, the more they flared;
From the beginning they grew ever stronger;
The more they died, the more they multiplied.
He poured blood into the black waters;
Behold how the son inherited
His father’s bloodthirstiness.
He broke through sands and made a road,
And attacked the frenzied foe.
He never retreated before death,
Nor turned back if gunfire meant dying.
Told to drink water, he drank poison;
Told to spill blood, he spilled his very soul.
Told to take a cap, he severed a head—
The offspring of the lion,
Who set the grassy steppe ablaze.
He was the true-born son
Of the finest stone-armored Chinese.
Hardened by entering battle,
He had won renown as a lion.
He had pledged himself to the twelve holy patrons;
God had fashioned him aright,
Favored him and opened his path.
When he struck stone, he never faltered;
No enemy survived facing him.
He turned pursued deer into cattle,
And made the whole world his subject.
He bore eighty-four pieces of armor;
Wherever he swept, there was fire.
Whoever faced him met destruction;
He loaded his bow with arrows
And annihilated all who fought him.
The lion’s own son,
The young prince,
Poor Khan Almambet.
He furiously attacked,
Kindling a fierce and violent struggle.
The horse he rode was Surkoon,
With mattock-like hooves and a broad rump,
A stallion fit for open country.
Ridden into combat, it never flinched;
Ridden on a raid, it never ached.
Ridden scouting, it never tired;
Ridden into battle, it never faltered.
With a broad rump and owl-like feet,
It never wearied when ridden into combat.
Its tail streamed like a parrot’s;
Though the road were ninety days long,
It galloped without stopping.
That creature Surkoon
Had endured ninety battles
Of turmoil across the hills.
When a spear was thrust, it darted aside;
When a battle-axe fell, the brute
Suddenly swerved the other way.
Such was its habit against the foe.
“The prancing beast
Is about to fall,” he said,
And with a shout thrust his spear.
Your hero, the ogre’s son,
Did not flinch, standing firm as iron;
He counted the boy’s thrust spear
As no more than the hem of his robe.
He found its true measure,
Seized the outstretched spear,
Snapped it at the middle,
And chopped it into twelve pieces.
“Come, you celebrated champion!” he cried.
“Come, you mighty warrior!
If your youth cannot come, let your elders come;
Let the strongest of you all come!
Leave the rest—let your khan come;
Let every Kyrgyz swarm upon me!
I will not cease speaking the truth.
I shall strip away your strength,
And swallow your blood like kumis.
Not leaving even a hair of you,
I shall slaughter you all!
When I roar, most of you will die;
If by chance I pounce,
You will go where none return—
Then you will behold my brutality!”
Thus he stood boasting of his valor.
God Almighty had struck
The infidel son of an ogre.
When Külchoro heard this—
Külchoro, whose fortune was complete,
Who was a steel bullet against the foe,
A glowing bed of crimson coals,
Whose equal did not exist among all men,
Whose fortune was complete—
He was descended from his father Almambet,
A lion born greater than his sire.
His father was gray-maned Almambet,
Descendant of the strongest
Among the armor-wearing Chinese.
When he charged shouting, no spear pierced him;
Those who grappled could not reach him.
None proved strong enough to trade blows;
No man defeated him in combat.
Could any man bend down and seize him?
Could anyone who faced him remain alive?
The infidel son of an ogre
Would not sink if cast into a river,
Nor be swept away by a flood.
He did not burn when engulfed by fire,
Nor die beneath a hail of bullets.
Even a slashing sword could not cut him;
The fearsome infidel’s body
Could not be pierced by showers of bullets.
He was one who had been scorched by fire,
With the eyes of a black demon.
Was he a foe created
To inflict suffering upon mankind?
A mountain with broad slopes,
Which no mattock could ever wear away.
He was a dreadful mountain pass
Beyond the strength of man.
He was a wind from Mount Kap
That leveled the whole world.
